claims.claim: Direct activators of Arp2/3 activity—WASP and the WAVE regulatory complex—form dynamic, linear arcs that propagate like traveling waves when observed at the cell surface by TIRF microscopy.
claims.source: This model for the assembly of flat pseudopods is supported by previous observations that activators of Arp2/3-dependent actin assembly appear in linear patterns on the membrane. When observed at the cell surface by TIRF microscopy, direct activators of Arp2/3 activity—WASP and the WAVE regulatory complex—form dynamic, linear arcs that propagate like traveling waves (Weiner et al., 2007; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weiner et al., 2007 and Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017, which describe WAVE and WASP localization patterns.

claims.claim: Only WASP and WAVE have been shown to form lines, while further upstream components of the activation cascade, such as Rac, exhibit more diffuse localization patterns.
claims.source: To date, only these two Arp2/3 activators have been shown to form lines, while further upstream components of the activation cascade, such as Rac, exhibit more diffuse localization patterns (Weiner et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Weiner et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2016, which describe localization patterns of different signaling molecules.

claims.claim: Multiple dynamic Arp2/3 activation zones produce multiple lamellar pseudopods that can interact to form complex rosettes.
claims.source: We propose that these multiple dynamic Arp2/3 activation zones produce multiple lamellar pseudopods that can interact to form complex rosettes.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on observations of WAVE complex localization and pseudopod morphology.

claims.claim: Membrane-bound circles of WAVE complex initiate formation of cylindrical, cup-like protrusions during macropinocytosis in Dictyostelium cells.
claims.source: Similarly, recent lattice light sheet microscopy of Dictyostelium cells revealed membrane-bound circles of WAVE complex (known as SCAR in Dictyostelium) initiating formation of cylindrical, cup-like protrusions during macropinocytosis (Veltman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Veltman et al., 2016, which describes WAVE/SCAR localization during macropinocytosis.

claims.claim: Cells that produce only a single, stable line of Arp2/3 activators at the leading edge produce only a single lamellar protrusion.
claims.source: In contrast, cells that produce only a single, stable line of Arp2/3 activators at the leading edge (e.g. Drosophila S2 cells [Kunda et al., 2003] and epithelial cells [Gautier et al., 2011]) produce only a single lamellar protrusion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kunda et al., 2003 and Gautier et al., 2011, which describe Arp2/3 activator localization in different cell types.

claims.claim: Complex pseudopods are not required for HL-60 cell migration, but they do play a role in direction change.
claims.source: We find that although complex pseudopods are not required for HL-60 cell migration, they do play a role in direction change.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing that CK-666 treated cells can migrate but turn less frequently.

claims.claim: The size and number of membrane protrusions increase dramatically when cells change direction.
claims.source: Using automated methods to detect and measure pseudopods we find that the size and number of these membrane protrusions increase dramatically when cells change direction and that blocking pseudopod formation reduces the frequency of direction changes (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6 correlating pseudopod dynamics with cell turning.

claims.claim: Blocking pseudopod formation reduces the frequency of direction changes.
claims.source: Using automated methods to detect and measure pseudopods we find that the size and number of these membrane protrusions increase dramatically when cells change direction and that blocking pseudopod formation reduces the frequency of direction changes (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced turning frequency in CK-666 treated cells, shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Reducing WAVE activity in dendritic cells abolishes pseudopod formation, yet accelerates the crawling of cells in simple confined spaces.
claims.source: These results provide a simple explanation for recent work from the Sixt lab, who found that reducing WAVE activity in dendritic cells abolishes pseudopod formation, yet accelerates the crawling of cells in simple confined spaces (Leithner et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leithner et al., 2016, which describes effects of WAVE inhibition on dendritic cell migration.

claims.claim: Pseudopod-deficient dendritic cells fail to reorient in changing gradients of chemoattractant.
claims.source: Interestingly, the pseudopod-deficient dendritic cells fail to reorient in changing gradients of chemoattractant, and migrate more slowly toward a chemotactic source within complex three-dimensional environments compared to control cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from Leithner et al., 2016, describing behavior of WAVE-inhibited dendritic cells.

claims.claim: Arp2/3 activity at the front of migrating dendritic cells is responsible for speed-fluctuating behavior.
claims.source: Similarly, in another recent paper, the Piel and Lennon-Dumenil labs found that Arp2/3 activity at the front of migrating dendritic cells was responsible for speed-fluctuating behavior (Vargas et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vargas et al., 2016, which describes the role of Arp2/3 in dendritic cell migration dynamics.

claims.claim: The three-dimensional pseudopods produced by fast-moving leukocytes promote the cell turning required for exploration of the local environment.
claims.source: Together with these findings in dendritic cells, our results suggest that the three-dimensional pseudopods produced by fast-moving leukocytes promote the cell turning required for exploration of the local environment.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the authors' data combined with findings from other studies on dendritic cells.

claims.claim: A pseudopodial sheet is much thinner than a spherical bleb but can sweep out a comparable volume.
claims.source: We speculate that broad, lamellar pseudopodia and extended rosettes may be uniquely adept structures for probing a cell's environment. A pseudopodial sheet is much thinner than a spherical bleb but can sweep out a comparable volume.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about the functional advantages of lamellar pseudopods based on their geometric properties.

claims.claim: Linear filopodia would have to move both back and forth and side to side to search the same volume as a lamellar sheet, and would provide limited surface contact.
claims.source: Linear filopodia, in contrast, would have to move both back and forth and side to side to search the same volume, and would provide limited surface contact.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation about the relative efficiency of different protrusion types for environmental exploration.

claims.claim: UCSF Chimera is a freely available, open-source software platform developed to render and analyze three-dimensional atomic structures and density maps.
claims.source: UCSF Chimera is a freely available, open-source software platform developed to render and analyze three-dimensional atomic structures (Pettersen et al., 2004) and density maps (Goddard et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pettersen et al., 2004 and Goddard et al., 2007, which describe UCSF Chimera software.

claims.claim: The loss of Arp2/3 activity dramatically reduced adhesion of HL-60 cells to fibronectin-coated coverslips.
claims.source: This analysis was limited to cells moving through three-dimensional collagen matrices because we found that the loss of Arp2/3 activity dramatically reduced adhesion of HL-60 cells to fibronectin-coated coverslips.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations that CK-666 treated cells did not adhere well to coverslips.

claims.claim: While control cells built lamellar pseudopods, CK-666 treated cells formed long, tubular protrusions.
claims.source: While control cells built lamellar pseudopods, CK-666 treated cells formed long, tubular protrusions (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B comparing control and CK-666 treated cells.

claims.claim: The absence of fluorescent utrophin from membrane-proximal regions of the cell provides a convenient marker to identify protrusions driven by the growth of branched actin networks.
claims.source: We used the absence of fluorescent utrophin from membrane-proximal regions of the cell as a convenient marker to identify protrusions driven by the growth of branched actin networks, and automated this process by subtracting the volume enclosed by a utrophin-based actin probe from the volume enclosed by the plasma membrane marker (Figure 6A, Video 14).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the method developed by the authors for automated pseudopod detection, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Time-lapse sequences generated by the lattice light sheet microscope comprised two-color image stacks, collected through entire cell volumes at 1.3 s intervals with minimal photobleaching and no evidence of phototoxicity.
claims.source: Time-lapse sequences generated by the lattice light sheet microscope comprised two-color image stacks, collected through entire cell volumes at 1.3 s intervals with minimal photobleaching and no evidence of phototoxicity.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the technical capabilities of the lattice light sheet microscope used in the study.

claims.claim: Lamellar pseudopods maintained an approximately constant thickness throughout their lifetime.
claims.source: Despite being unsupported, these pseudopods maintained a lamellar morphology with an approximately constant thickness throughout their lifetime (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2E tracking pseudopod thickness over time.

claims.claim: Lamellar pseudopods have a similar profile whether cells crawl across glass or through a collagen matrix.
claims.source: Regardless of whether cells crawled across glass or through a collagen matrix, their lamellar pseudopods shared several common features, including a similar profile (Figure 2C) and thickness (780 ± 137 nm standard deviation, n = 18 cells).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C comparing pseudopods in different environments.

claims.claim: Lamellar pseudopods have a thickness of 780 ± 137 nm (standard deviation, n = 18 cells) when measured from surface-rendered LLSm data.
claims.source: Regardless of whether cells crawled across glass or through a collagen matrix, their lamellar pseudopods shared several common features, including a similar profile (Figure 2C) and thickness (780 ± 137 nm standard deviation, n = 18 cells).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on quantitative measurements of pseudopod thickness from lattice light sheet microscopy data.

claims.claim: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen).
claims.source: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including: raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen); spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin (505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal); and scanning electron micrographs, which suggest a thickness of ~640 nm (Fleck et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on measurements from multiple imaging modalities, providing convergent evidence for pseudopod thickness.

claims.claim: Spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin show pseudopod thickness of 505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal.
claims.source: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including: raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen); spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin (505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal); and scanning electron micrographs, which suggest a thickness of ~640 nm (Fleck et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on measurements from confocal microscopy of fixed, phalloidin-stained cells.

claims.claim: Scanning electron micrographs suggest a pseudopod thickness of ~640 nm.
claims.source: The thickness measured from surface-rendered LLSm data agrees with measurements made on other types of data, including: raw lattice light sheet data (567 ± 64 nm on glass and 689 ± 86 nm in collagen); spinning disk confocal images of phalloidin-stained actin (505 ± 49 nm for a sheet and 533 ± 123 nm for a rosette petal); and scanning electron micrographs, which suggest a thickness of ~640 nm (Fleck et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on measurements from scanning electron micrographs, with citation to Fleck et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Lamellar pseudopods are not perfectly flat, and exhibit varying degrees of pucker and undulation.
claims.source: Lamellar pseudopods are not perfectly flat, and exhibit varying degrees of pucker and undulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from three-dimensional imaging of pseudopod morphology.

claims.claim: In uniform fields of chemoattractant, both lamellar and rosette pseudopods are highly dynamic and ephemeral.
claims.source: In uniform fields of chemoattractant, both lamellar and rosette pseudopods are highly dynamic and ephemeral (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Ambient occlusion tonal surface rendering makes cellular structures more easily interpretable by emphasizing the spatial relationships of three-dimensional surfaces and variations in surface texture.
claims.source: Tonal surface rendering with ambient occlusion makes cellular structures more easily interpretable by emphasizing the spatial relationships of three-dimensional surfaces and variations in surface texture.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the benefits of the ambient occlusion rendering technique used in the study.

claims.claim: The enhanced ability to detect and interpret textures and protrusions can be seen by comparing traditional maximum intensity projection and rendered versions of confocal data.
claims.source: The enhanced ability to detect and interpret textures and protrusions can be seen by comparing traditional maximum intensity projection and rendered versions of confocal data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and similar renderings of the lattice light sheet data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparisons shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: HL-60 cells produce two distinctive types of dynamic membrane protrusion at the leading edge: thin, sheet-like lamina and 'rosettes' formed by the coincidence of multiple lamina.
claims.source: Using these visualization tools, we observed two distinctive types of dynamic membrane protrusion at the leading edge of HL-60 cells crawling on fibronectin-coated coverslips: (i) thin, sheet-like lamina (Figure 2 and Videos 1–6), and (ii) 'rosettes' formed by the coincidence of multiple lamina (Figure 3, Videos 7–10).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from lattice light sheet microscopy shown in Figures 2 and 3 and associated videos.

claims.claim: The morphology of lamellar and rosette protrusions differ from the spherical blebs produced when the plasma membrane detaches from the underlying cortex.
claims.source: The morphology of these protrusions differ from the spherical blebs produced when the plasma membrane detaches from the underlying cortex (Charras and Paluch, 2008), instead they resemble membrane movements driven by rapid assembly of filamentous actin.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on morphological observations and comparison to known characteristics of blebs, with citation to Charras and Paluch, 2008.

claims.claim: Leading-edge sheets and rosettes are filled with dense actin networks.
claims.source: Using confocal microscopy of fixed cells labeled with phalloidin, we verified that leading-edge sheets and rosettes are filled with dense actin networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data of phalloidin-stained cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Dynamic sheets and rosettes are readily apparent in surface renderings of three-dimensional lattice light sheet microscopy data, but are not easily identified in two-dimensional projections.
claims.source: Dynamic sheets and rosettes are readily apparent in surface renderings of three-dimensional lattice light sheet microscopy data, but are not easily identified in two-dimensional projections (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2), consistent with the failure of conventional light microscopy to identify these structures.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparisons shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2 demonstrating the advantage of 3D rendering.

claims.claim: Similar lamellar protrusions were observed in fixed Jurkat T cells using scanning electron microscopy.
claims.source: Using scanning electron microscopy, we observed similar lamellar protrusions in fixed Jurkat T cells, another amoeboid cell type that employs fast, low-adhesion crawling through complex environments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Pseudopodial sheets sometimes travel across the dorsal surface of the cell, from front to back or side to side.
claims.source: Lamellar pseudopods were not limited to the plane of the coverslip and, in three-dimensional movies, we observed many pseudopodial sheets travelling across the dorsal surface of the cell, from front to back (Figure 2A and Video 1) or side to side (Video 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse lattice light sheet microscopy shown in Figure 2A and Videos 1-2.

claims.claim: Most pseudopodial sheets emerged from the cell body and projected directly into the liquid medium without ever contacting the surface of the coverslip.
claims.source: Importantly, most pseudopodial sheets emerged from the cell body and projected directly into the liquid medium without ever contacting the surface of the coverslip (Videos 3 and 4 and time overlay in Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse imaging shown in Videos 3 and 4 and Figure 2A.

results.result: Lattice light sheet microscopy (LLSm) provides high spatial resolution (~230 nm XY, ~370 nm Z), high temporal resolution (1.3 s intervals), and low phototoxicity for 3D imaging of living cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C16, and C75 collectively establish the technical capabilities of LLSm. The resolution specifications are supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014, and the temporal resolution and lack of phototoxicity are demonstrated through the experimental data collection parameters described in the methods.

results.result: The utrophin-based actin probe selectively labels cortical actin while being excluded from dynamic pseudopod actin networks, enabling automated pseudopod detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C19, and C74 establish the specificity of the utrophin probe. The preferential binding to cortical actin is supported by citation to Belin et al., 2014, and exclusion from pseudopods is demonstrated in Figure 1B. The utility for automated detection is shown in Figure 6A.

results.result: HL-60 cell pseudopods contain dense polymerized actin networks as visualized by phalloidin staining in fixed cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C88 are supported by confocal microscopy data of phalloidin-stained fixed cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, providing direct evidence of actin content in pseudopods.

results.result: Three-dimensional pseudopods are composed of thin (430-800 nm), flat lamellar sheets that can exist as isolated structures or interleave to form rosette structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C17, C41, C42, and C78-C81 establish pseudopod morphology through convergent measurements from multiple imaging modalities (LLSm, confocal, SEM). The thickness measurements are consistent across techniques (505-780 nm), and the lamellar and rosette morphologies are clearly demonstrated in Figures 2 and 3.

results.result: Lamellar pseudopods maintain their flat morphology independent of external surface contact, as demonstrated by free-standing sheets in 3D collagen matrices and sheets projecting into liquid medium.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C18, C43, C45, and C92 demonstrate that pseudopod flatness is intrinsic rather than templated by surfaces. Figure 2D shows similar flatness in 2D and 3D environments, and Videos 3-4 show free-standing sheets. This is a key finding that distinguishes these structures from adherent lamellipodia.

results.result: Pseudopods are Arp2/3-dependent structures that disappear upon CK-666 treatment, with pseudopod volume decreasing by 40% and formation rate dropping from 1.9 to 0.8 pseudopods/min.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C21, C34, C35, and C73 establish Arp2/3 dependence through pharmacological inhibition. Figure 4B and Videos 11-12 show loss of lamellar pseudopods, and quantitative analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C demonstrates the 40% volume reduction. The formation rate data is based on manual counting from time-lapse sequences.

results.result: Sheet and rosette pseudopods share common structural and dynamic properties: similar thickness (690±20 nm), ~60 s lifespan independent of environment, constant thickness during lifetime, and ~75% collapse into filopodia-like structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 and C76 establish that sheets and rosettes are variants of the same structural motif. Thickness measurements (Figure 3B), lifespan data (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), and collapse behavior (Figure 3E, Video 1) provide strong evidence. The independence from mechanical support is inferred from similar lifespans in 2D vs 3D.

results.result: Lamellar pseudopods initiate as linear ridges on the plasma membrane and grow at 11.9±5.4 µm/min while maintaining a linear distal edge.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 describe pseudopod formation dynamics based on time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3C. The growth rate is quantified from n=4 measurements. However, the small sample size (n=4) for the growth rate measurement is a limitation.

results.result: WAVE complex forms linear arcs that co-localize with moving lines of close cell-coverslip contact, suggesting that TIRF 'waves' represent edges of lamellar sheets pressed against the coverslip.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 integrate prior TIRF observations (Weiner et al., 2007) with new RICM data. Figure 5 and Video 13 show co-localization of WAVE complex with regions of close contact. Claim C30 is an inference connecting these observations to the lamellar structure, which is reasonable but not directly proven.

results.result: Arp2/3-dependent pseudopods are dispensable for 3D migration, as CK-666 treated cells retain motility but move more slowly (5.42 vs 8.57 µm/min).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C36, C37, and C62 demonstrate that pseudopods are not absolutely required for migration. CK-666 treated cells continue to migrate through collagen (Videos 11-12), though more slowly (Figure 6E). The speed reduction is statistically significant (p=0.024).

results.result: Elimination of Arp2/3-dependent pseudopods dramatically reduces cell turning frequency by 2-3 fold (from 2.73-3.41 to 1.09-1.15 turns/min depending on method).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C38, and C64 establish the role of pseudopods in directional changes. Two independent quantification methods (Figure 6D-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) show consistent 2-3 fold reductions in turning frequency, providing robust evidence.

results.result: Pseudopod dynamics increase dramatically when cells change direction, with size and number of protrusions correlating with turning events.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C39, and C63 establish the correlation between pseudopod activity and turning. Figure 6B visualizes this relationship by overlaying pseudopod dynamics on cell trajectories. However, correlation does not establish causation, and the temporal relationship could be examined more rigorously.

results.result: Control cells build pseudopods preferentially in the direction of motion, while CK-666 treated cells show more uniform pseudopod distribution.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is supported by directional analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B. This suggests pseudopods play a role in directional sensing or steering, though the mechanism is not explored.

results.result: Similar lamellar and rosette structures have been observed in multiple cell types including neutrophils, T cells, dendritic cells, monocytes, and Dictyostelium, as documented in published electron micrographs.
results.evaluation: Claims C44 and C90 are supported by citations to multiple published studies and new SEM data of Jurkat T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). This suggests the lamellar pseudopod architecture may be a general feature of fast-moving amoeboid cells.

results.result: Complex three-dimensional pseudopods can be resolved into lamellar components.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by observations that rosette pseudopods are composed of multiple interleaved lamellar sheets (Figures 3, Videos 7-10). This represents a key conceptual advance in understanding pseudopod architecture.

results.result: Free-standing pseudopodial sheets are thicker (430-800 nm vs <200 nm) and grow faster than attached lamellipodia.
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C48 compare pseudopods to lamellipodia based on measurements and citations to Abercrombie et al., 1971 and Ingram, 1969. The thickness comparison is well-supported, though the growth rate comparison relies on historical literature and may not reflect identical experimental conditions.

results.result: The dimensionality of actin network protrusions is determined by the dimensionality of Arp2/3 activator organization: point sources (0D) generate filopodia (1D), line sources (1D) generate lamellar sheets (2D), and area sources (2D) generate 3D structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C56 propose a model based on in vitro reconstitution studies (C50-C52) and generalize to a dimensional rule (C53-C55). While the in vitro evidence is cited, the generalization (C53) and application to pseudopods (C56) are speculative. The model is plausible and supported by analogy, but lacks direct experimental validation in cells.

results.result: WASP and WAVE form dynamic linear arcs at the cell surface, while upstream regulators like Rac show diffuse patterns; multiple linear activation zones are proposed to generate multiple lamellar pseudopods that form rosettes.
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C58 are supported by citations to Weiner et al., 2007, Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017, and Yang et al., 2016. Claim C59 is a proposed model connecting linear WAVE organization to rosette formation, which is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Different patterns of Arp2/3 activator organization correlate with different protrusion morphologies: circular WAVE patterns produce cylindrical cups (macropinocytosis), single stable lines produce single lamellae, and multiple dynamic lines produce rosettes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60 and C61 are supported by citations to Veltman et al., 2016, Kunda et al., 2003, and Gautier et al., 2011. This comparative analysis across cell types strengthens the dimensional organization model, though it remains correlative.

results.result: Studies in dendritic cells show that reducing WAVE/Arp2/3 activity abolishes pseudopods, accelerates migration in simple environments, but impairs reorientation in gradients and navigation in complex environments, supporting a role for pseudopods in pathfinding.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 accurately cite findings from Leithner et al., 2016 and Vargas et al., 2016. Claim C68 integrates these findings with the authors' data to propose a pathfinding role, which is a reasonable inference supported by the correlation between pseudopod dynamics and turning.

results.result: Lamellar pseudopods may be more efficient than blebs or filopodia for environmental exploration because sheets can sweep large volumes while maintaining surface contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C70 are explicitly speculative geometric arguments about functional advantages. While the geometric reasoning is sound, there is no experimental evidence testing these hypotheses. This represents interesting speculation for future work.

results.result: UCSF Chimera with ambient occlusion rendering enables superior visualization and interpretation of 3D cellular structures compared to traditional maximum intensity projections, revealing pseudopod morphology not apparent in 2D projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C84, C85, and C89 describe the visualization methodology. The superiority of 3D rendering is demonstrated by direct comparisons in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2. This represents an important methodological contribution.

results.result: Loss of Arp2/3 activity dramatically reduced HL-60 cell adhesion to fibronectin-coated coverslips.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is based on observations that necessitated limiting analysis to 3D collagen matrices. While not quantified, this observation is consistent with known roles of Arp2/3 in adhesion.

results.result: Lamellar pseudopods are not perfectly flat and exhibit varying degrees of pucker and undulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is based on 3D imaging observations and is consistent with the flatness measurements in Figure 2D showing some variability. This qualifies the 'flat sheet' description appropriately.

results.result: In uniform chemoattractant fields, both lamellar and rosette pseudopods are highly dynamic and ephemeral.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by time-lapse observations in Figure 4A showing rapid pseudopod turnover. The ~60 s lifespan (C23) quantifies this dynamic behavior.

results.result: HL-60 cells produce two types of dynamic membrane protrusions—lamellar sheets and rosettes—that differ morphologically from spherical blebs and resemble actin-driven structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C86 and C87 are supported by observations in Figures 2-3 and comparison to known bleb morphology (citation to Charras and Paluch, 2008). The actin content is confirmed by phalloidin staining.

results.result: Pseudopodial sheets travel across the dorsal cell surface from front to back or side to side.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is supported by 3D time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2A and Videos 1-2. This demonstrates that pseudopods are not restricted to the ventral surface.

results.result: Lamellar pseudopods have similar profiles whether cells crawl on glass or through collagen matrices.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 is supported by imaging data in Figure 2C comparing pseudopods in different environments. This reinforces that pseudopod morphology is intrinsic.

results.result: Background on cell migration modes: adhesion-based migration (restricted to animals, driven by Arp2/3-dependent lamellipodia) versus fast adhesion-independent migration (ancestral, several orders of magnitude faster, associated with complex 3D pseudopods that may function more in exploration than propulsion).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C15 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. Claim C15 is an inference from prior work (Leithner et al., 2016; Vargas et al., 2016) that motivates the current study.
